description: Normative global 1.5°C pathway led by behaviour-driven low energy demand; REMIND-MAgPIE 3.3.
pathwayDescription:
The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) develops reference climate scenarios to help central banks, regulators, and financial institutions assess transition and physical risks associated with climate change. The Low Demand, REMIND-MAgPIE 3.3-4.8 (LD REMIND) scenario describes a world in which strong climate policies are combined with major shifts in behavior, energy efficiency, and consumption patterns, resulting in significantly lower energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions. This scenario assumes widespread adoption of sustainable lifestyles, efficiency gains across all sectors, and rapid deployment of mature low-carbon technologies. As a result, global energy demand peaks early and declines steadily through the century.

The LD REMIND pathway achieves a 1.1°C temperature outcome by 2100, more ambitious than the Net Zero 2050 scenario, and with less reliance on carbon dioxide removal and negative-emission technologies. The scenario emphasizes demand-side mitigation, reflecting both behavioral change and systemic efficiency improvements rather than purely supply-side transformation. It is the most ambitious of the pathways published by NGFS.

This scenario is one of seven scenarios published by NGFS. Note that all NGFS scenarios are produced using three different Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs): REMIND-MAgPIE, MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM, and GCAM. These IAMs share the common assumptions that define each scenario, but may offer different projections based on underlying model structure. Technical users may wish to consult NGFS documentation to determine if a specific IAM best fits their applications.

coreDrivers.policies: Carbon price: the shadow carbon price reaches 111 US$2010/tCO2 in 2030 and 487 in 2050, the main lever moving investment and dispatch away from fossil fuels. Other: fossil-gas import restrictions constrain Europe's gas supply.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Same 1.5°C / net-zero-CO2-around-2050 constraint as Net Zero 2050 with national net-zero targets met; lower demand reduces the carbon price needed. REMIND applies the targets by its 12 regions (e.g. India as CO2-only).
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: REMIND optimises intertemporally over investment, O&M, fuel and emission costs, with adjustment costs on fast scale-up. Learning cuts solar PV from 866 to 361 US$2010/kW by 2050 here, so cost decline depends on deployment: wind and solar reach 79% of 2050 generation (Current Policies 72%). With carbon at 487 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050, the cost ranking tilts further to low-carbon options.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon power investment moves from 0.99% of GDP (MER) in 2020 to 0.81% in 2050, a decrease of 19%. Investment and GDP are solved jointly in REMIND's general equilibrium.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Shared SSP2 v3.0 population and GDP drive energy and material demand: 9.64 billion people in 2050 and GDP (MER) growing 2.23%/yr over 2020-2050. The assumptions are common to all NGFS scenarios; GDP differs from Current Policies only through transition costs (-1.25% in 2050).
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: Behavioural change lowers energy demand: 2050 final energy is 270 EJ vs 386 EJ in Net Zero 2050 (-30%), cutting the 2050 carbon price to 487 from 749 US$2010/tCO2. Passenger aviation is 8240 vs 9350 bn pkm.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Limited carbon dioxide removal: REMIND switches off direct air capture and enhanced weathering, forcing deeper gross cuts and higher carbon prices (487 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050; total CCS 3019 Mt CO2/yr). It is a technology-availability limit, not a cost, policy or target, so no other driver fits.

dependencies.dependency_description: Grid decarbonisation in Low Demand (REMIND) rests on the carbon price (111 US$2010/tCO2 in 2030, 487 in 2050). It lifts wind and solar from 10% of generation in 2020 to 79% in 2050 and cuts coal capacity to 1% of its 2020 level by 2040.

Power investment averages 1631 bn US$2010/yr over 2025-2050 (0.99x Current Policies), including 721 bn/yr for grids, and must be financed. A 2050 carbon price of 487 US$2010/tCO2 erodes unabated fossil plant profitability.

Low Demand (REMIND) assumes behavioural cuts in energy demand, so 2050 generation is 174 EJ vs 270 EJ in Net Zero 2050 (-35%). Lower demand eases the renewable build-out; the shift is an imposed scenario assumption, not a modelled consumer response.

With wind and solar at 79% of 2050 generation, grids, storage and flexibility must absorb variable output. REMIND prices batteries, hydrogen storage, grid expansion and curtailment as integration costs; storage reaches 5116 GW by 2050. Grid investment averages 721 bn US$2010/yr (2025-2050). No hourly dispatch is reported, so curtailment cannot be checked.

Power CCS captures 173 Mt CO2/yr in 2050 (172 Mt from bioenergy), so the pathway needs CCS at commercial scale; CCS cost differences between models drive large gaps in fossil generation. Storage of 5116 GW in 2050 relies on continued storage cost declines (endogenous learning).

REMIND uses regional renewable potentials by grade (hydro capped near 50 EJ/yr) and MAgPIE biomass competing with food. Power BECCS reaches 172 Mt CO2/yr and primary biomass 70 EJ in 2050, so land limits the negative-emission part of the power transition. Wind and solar at 79% of 174 EJ draw on the regional potentials.

Steel decarbonisation in Low Demand (REMIND) is steered only through economy-wide carbon pricing (487 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050) and emissions constraints; no steel-specific industrial policy is described. Steel emissions change by -103% over 2020-2050.

At 487 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050, fossil ironmaking costs more, favouring electricity (2.7 EJ) and hydrogen (1.7 EJ) in steel in 2050. No steel investment or unit-cost data are reported, so financing needs cannot be quantified.

Behavioural and material-efficiency assumptions in Low Demand (REMIND) cut 2050 crude steel to 536 Mt vs 1779 Mt in Net Zero 2050 (-70%), shrinking the output that must be decarbonised. The cut is an imposed demand assumption.

Hydrogen supplies 24% of steel final energy in 2050 in Low Demand (REMIND), so hydrogen production, transport and storage must reach steel sites. Economy-wide CO2 transport and storage investment is 18 bn US$2010/yr in 2050, none attributed to steel.
Hydrogen-based ironmaking must scale to 1.7 EJ (24% of steel energy) by 2050 in Low Demand (REMIND). It is not yet market-ready, and the documentation states no readiness or efficiency assumptions.

The only policy acting on aviation in Low Demand (REMIND) is the carbon price on transport fuel (487 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050); no aviation mandate such as SAF blending is represented. Passenger aviation goes from 6910 to 8240 bn pkm over 2020-2050.
Carbon-priced fuel holds 2050 passenger aviation to 45% of the Current Policies level (8240 vs 18312 bn pkm), so demand responds through price rather than fuel switching.
Low Demand (REMIND) assumes behavioural cuts in travel, so 2050 passenger aviation is 8240 vs 9350 bn pkm in Net Zero 2050 (-12%). Demand restraint is a main mitigation route for aviation here.
